questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡y & =x+C \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡y & =-x-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=\frac{\pi }{2}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-0-C \\ 0 & =0-C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡y=-x
$$

questions.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation
$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4x\sqrt{y}$
that satisfies the condition $y(1)=9.$  Assume that $y>0.$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =4x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 4x\,\text{d}x \\ 2\sqrt{y} & =2{x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \sqrt{y} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\ y & ={({x}^{2}+\frac{{C}_{1}}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming $y>0,$ the general solution is

$$
y(x)=({x}^{2}+C)^{2},
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=9$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =((1)^{2}+C)^{2} \\ 9 & =(1+C)^{2} \\ 3 & =1+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=({x}^{2}+2)^{2}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =xy \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/2+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/2+C}\, \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}/2+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}/2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(0)=1$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =K{e}^{0} \\ K & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=xy$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{{x}^{2}/2}\,.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-\frac{1}{x}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-1/x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-1/x+C}\, \\ |y| & ={e}^{-1/x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =K{e}^{-1/x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(1)=e$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}e & =K{e}^{-1} \\ K & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}=0$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=e$ is

$$
y={e}^{2-1/x}\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y{e}^{-x}$ that satisfies $y(0)={e}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,dx & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =-{e}^{-x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{-{e}^{-x}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{-{e}^{-x}+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{-{e}^{-x}+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{-{e}^{-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(0)={e}^{-1}$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-1} & =K{e}^{-{e}^{-0}} \\ {e}^{-1} & =K{e}^{-1} \\ K & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y{e}^{-x}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)={e}^{-1}$ is

$$
y={e}^{-{e}^{-x}}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ that satisfies $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={\pi }^{2}.$ Assume that $0<x<\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x+8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+8x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+8x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x+8\int x\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x+4{x}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the right-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0.$

Hence,

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+4{x}^{2}+C.
$$

where $C={C}_{1}+{C}_{2}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={\pi }^{2}$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})+4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1+{\pi }^{2}+C & ={\pi }^{2} \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8x\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ that satisfies the condition $y(\frac{\pi }{2})={\pi }^{2}$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+4{x}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies $y(1)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y} & =4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}-{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(4{x}^{3}-1){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}-1 \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (4{x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={x}^{4}-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{4}-1+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =0 \\ C & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y}=4{x}^{3}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=0$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}-x+1).
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x}=3$ that satisfies $y(0)=-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3+2x{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{e}^{-x}+2x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{e}^{-x}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int 3{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x+\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-3{e}^{-x}+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=-3$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =-3 \\ -3{e}^{-0}+{0}^{2}+C & =-3 \\ C-3 & =-3 \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of ${e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x}=3$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=-3$ is

$$
y={x}^{2}-3{e}^{-x}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+{y}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(-1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{1}{x}+x+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}-Cx}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{1-{x}^{2}-Cx}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{1-{x}^{2}-Cx},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(-1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(-1) & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{1-(-1)^{2}-C(-1)} & =1 \\ \frac{-1}{C} & =1 \\ C & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+{y}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(-1)=1$ is

$$
y=\frac{x}{1+x-{x}^{2}}\,.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-{e}^{-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{0}+C) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ C-1 & =\frac{1}{4} \\ C & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-x-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{5}{4}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $y' = 5y$ that satisfies $y(0)=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5y \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5 \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =5x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm {e}^{5x+C} \\  & =\pm {e}^{C}{e}^{5x} \\  & =K{e}^{5x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm e^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

Now we apply the condition $y(0) = 3$ to find $K\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3 \\ K{e}^{5\cdot 0} & =3 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $y' = 5y$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=3$ is

$$
y = 3 e^{5x}  \,.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\cos(3y)\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \sin(2x) = 0$ given that  $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0.$ Assume that $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} < y < \dfrac{\pi}{6} .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\,\text{d}y & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1=3C.$

Now let's apply the condition $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0$ to find $C_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =0+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\sin(3y)   =  \dfrac {3} {2} \cos(2x)
$$
